# Analysis {#sec-analysis}

## Panel regression

The four task group values described in @eq-group sum to one, so all four cannot enter a
regression together. One serves as the reference category, and we use non routine
cognitive. Each remaining coefficient reads as the change in affordability salary
associated with a one percentage point shift out of non routine cognitive work and into
that group, holding the controls fixed. No coefficient stands alone; every one is a
comparison against the reference.

Normalizing the four totals by their sum, as @sec-data describes, also resolves a
collinearity problem that would otherwise make these coefficients unusable. The
unnormalized totals in @eq-weighted carry variance inflation factors between 13 and 27,
because occupations differ in how much total O*NET rating mass they hold and that inflates
all four totals together. Dividing by the four group sum removes the common scale and
drops the variance inflation factors to roughly 1.

Year indicators absorb conditions common to all counties within a year, including the 2008
recession, the recovery through the 2010s, and the price movement that affordability
salary does not itself deflate. Standard errors are clustered by county, since repeated
observations of the same county across fifteen years are not independent draws.

## Validation before modeling

Before estimating anything we confirm the data support the methods. We check the
distributions of the four task groups and of affordability salary for skew and outliers,
confirm county year coverage across the retained panel, and check the overlap between task
groups to make sure no two carry effectively the same information. @fig-dists shows the
distributions.

<!-- FIGURE: fig-dists. Histograms of affordability salary and the four task groups,
     small multiples. Purpose is to justify the modeling choices that follow, not to
     describe the data for its own sake. -->

Affordability salary is
right skewed, with most counties between \$40,000 and \$60,000 and a long tail reaching
toward \$160,000 driven by high income metropolitan counties [TK: confirm against the
current panel, these figures come from the earlier full frame]. That skew is the reason
the extremes of the distribution are worth watching in the specification check below.

## Specification check

A linear model assumes the association holds at a constant rate across the range of the
data. We test that with a RESET test, which adds powers of the fitted values to the
regression and asks whether they carry explanatory weight. [TK: report the statistic and p
value.] The linear specification is rejected. @fig-resid-analysis plots residuals against
fitted values and locates the failure: the association bends at the extremes of the
affordability distribution rather than holding constant across it.

<!-- FIGURE: fig-resid-analysis. Residuals against fitted values from the linear panel
     model, reference line at zero. This is the diagnostic that motivates everything
     after it. Decide whether it lives here as evidence for the specification check or
     in _05 as a result. -->

That rejection is a result rather than a discarded attempt. The linear model still
delivers the interpretable effect size we report, and it establishes through its own
diagnostics that the data hold structure a straight line cannot represent. Binned means
plots make the shape visible directly, and the flexible models take up what the linear
model leaves behind.

## Variance decomposition

Affordability salary varies both across counties and within a county over time, and the
two carry different implications. [TK: report the between and within split.] A county's
task mix moves very little across the panel, which is what makes the associated
affordability differences durable rather than transient.

<!-- FIGURE: fig-variance. Between and within variance split for affordability salary and
     for each of the four task groups. A simple grouped bar chart is enough. This is the
     figure that carries the persistence claim, which the conclusions lean on heavily, so
     it should not stay as a number in prose. -->

The Census occupation coding change between 2009 and 2010, described in @sec-data, inflates
apparent within county variation for the routine cognitive group. Because this is a
feature of how the source data were coded rather than a property of the counties, we
repeat the main estimates on a panel restricted to 2010 onward.

<!-- FIGURE: optional fig-coding-change. Routine cognitive group mean by year across the

## What these models can and cannot support

Every estimate reported here is associational. Counties are not assigned their mix of
work, and nothing in this design isolates a causal channel. A county with more routine
work also differs in industry structure, in the education of its workforce, and in its
housing market, and any of those could carry part of what we observe. We report which task
groups relate to affordability and how strongly, not what would follow if a county's mix
of work changed.
